source.title: Atlas-Alignment: Making Interpretability Transferable Across Language Models
source.authors: Bruno Puri; Jim Berend; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests indirect evidence for semantic features in LLM latent spaces through feature retrieval, using representational alignment rather than the original toy-network superposition method.
record.gate_note: The semantic retrieval evaluations test whether labeled atlas concepts can retrieve corresponding features in an LLM’s latent space. The paper also reports translation-quality and steering results, but translation quality is an intermediate alignment metric, and steering deliberately induces concept-related output; neither directly tests the claim versions at issue here. No experiment measures overcomplete sparse-feature storage geometry, neuron polysemanticity as a capacity effect, or spontaneous feature prevalence.
record.test_reason: A method paper. It uses a Gemma Scope SAE as a ready-made Concept Atlas and benchmarks five alignment methods (Covariance, Cross Corr., Linear Reg., Semantic Lens, Orth. Procrustes) for mapping other LLMs' activations into it. The retrieval results (Table 2, Table 8) score the study's own alignment methods. They do not measure how widely features are spread across neurons, whether a dictionary recovers sparse features, or any superposition geometry. The retrieved 'subject features' are Llama-IT layer-19 MLP neurons with descriptions taken from Choi et al., not dictionary features. High MRR means the alignment preserves concept identity; it says nothing about whether those neurons are superposed or polysemantic. No version's effect is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that lightweight linear alignment, especially Orthogonal Procrustes, to a labeled SAE-derived Concept Atlas enables semantic transfer, reliable concept retrieval and atlas-based steering across model families, amortizing interpretability cost. The retrieval evaluation itself covers only Llama-IT layer-19 MLP neurons (454 validated features). The authors make no claims about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses representational alignment from LLM activations to an SAE-derived concept space and evaluates semantic retrieval; it does not use the original toy-network superposition intervention or geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Retrieval changes substantially with alignment method and training-data size. The paper compares Gemma Scope 16k and 65k atlases in the main retrieval table.

fits_no_version.finding: An orthogonal rotation fitted on 500k shared sentences maps Gemma-2 SAE concept queries onto the matching Llama-IT L19 MLP neurons. Retrieval reaches MRR 0.97 against a random baseline of 0.015. Translation quality is above random for GPT-2, Qwen, Ministral and Llama variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model shared linear semantic structure: SAE concept directions from one LLM can be linearly aligned to units in other LLMs (Platonic or linear representation hypotheses).

record.problems: The quantitative retrieval evaluation is limited to Llama-IT layer 19 and 454 validated features; it depends on automatically generated concept sequences and feature descriptions. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The results do not measure superposition geometry or spontaneous feature prevalence.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were omitted. Translation-quality scores and concept-steering scores were not included because they do not directly measure the tested V4 feature-retrieval outcome described here.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweeps or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of other causes of polysemanticity.
Does not measure how features are distributed across neurons, and does not train or evaluate a dictionary's recovery of features. The Gemma Scope SAE is taken as given.

Uses SAE features as labeled units but does not test completeness, stability or canonicality. The 16k and 65k atlases give similar retrieval scores, but this is not framed as, or measured as, feature stability.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 link conflated 'retrieving labeled concepts in another model via alignment' with 'a dictionary recovers sparse features'. The paper assumes the SAE atlas is interpretable and monosemantic and builds on it as a tool, so it is T4. The translation-quality (Tables 1, 5–7) and steering (Tables 3, 10) results are likewise method benchmarks and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test overcomplete sparse feature storage, overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
Does not test whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.

Tests retrieval of semantically identified features in Llama-IT layer 19 using mapped Concept Atlas queries. Does not measure whether features are spread across many neurons, feature prevalence in LLMs generally, or recovery across the full range of models examined for translation quality.
Uses an SAE-derived Concept Atlas described as sparse and interpretable, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

relation.reason: Relies on SAE-derived interpretable features to transfer interpretability; does not independently test superposition or dictionary completeness, stability or canonicality.

tranche.reason: Uses an existing labeled Gemma Scope SAE atlas as a tool and evaluates alignment, retrieval and steering performance. These results do not test V1–V6.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled rows match the tables, but are method comparisons and should not count as superposition test evidence. The supplied text is v2 dated 24 Apr 2026; retrieval covers 454 validated Llama-IT layer-19 MLP features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama-IT layer 19, Orth. Procrustes, Gemma Scope 16k and 65k; and Orth. Procrustes with 10k–500k training samples
reader_labels.reason: Mapped atlas queries retrieve validated subject features strongly above random baselines (R9–R10, R36–R40). This supports feature recoverability in this tested model and setup, not feature spreading or prevalence across LLMs.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Alternative translation methods and low-data or method-dependent retrieval settings in Llama-IT layer 19
reader_labels.reason: Retrieval varies substantially by alignment method and training-data size; some methods are close to random, and 1k-sample Orth. Procrustes is weaker than at larger sizes (R1–R8, R11–R35).
